extracted.intended_audience: aspiring book reviewers and freelance writers who want to build a reviewing career or portfolio
extracted.subtask_description: A step-by-step how-to guide for people who want to start writing book reviews, build a portfolio, gain visibility, and pitch reviews to publications and platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read abundantly
rubrics_metrics.description: If you don’t already read like a maniac, then one might wonder why you’d want to become a book reviewer in the first place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be extremely well-read in the genres you plan to review so you can contextualize new books (e.g., know Stephen King for small-town New England horror). Read other book reviews to learn from the best. Reading under deadline becomes part of the job; breadth and depth of reading are core credentials for a critic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start reviewing (practice on retail sites and platforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin reviewing immediately by posting reviews on online retailers and joining review platforms (free or paid) to exercise your reviewing muscles and get visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write quality commentary on retail sites to gain feedback (e.g., 'X people found this helpful'). Consider paid editorial-review services (Kirkus, U.S. Review of Books, Online Book Club, Publisher’s Weekly) for free review copies but limited exposure. Join platforms like Reedsy Discovery for visibility and a reviewer landing page; expect some platforms to require writing samples for acceptance. Use templates if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always follow guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere closely to the submission and format guidelines of each review outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different outlets have strict formatting/length rules (Kirkus is cited as exacting). Following guidelines reduces rewrites, rejection, and editorial burden — editors appreciate reviewers whose copy requires little editing. Treat this as a professional habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think of the reader first
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on helping potential readers understand what the book is like rather than venting about a disliked book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a book in a way that gives a flavor of it (quotes, isolated sections). Highlight what will interest readers even in imperfect books. Avoid gratuitous evisceration; you can decline to review books that are utterly terrible. Aim to convince readers why they might enjoy the title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host all your reviews in one place
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a single online home for your reviews so you can easily share your portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a personal website, blog, or use a platform-provided landing page. A single URL for your back-catalog is useful when applying for reviewing jobs or pitching editors. This central repository should showcase your range and best work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Become a specialist
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on a few genres you know intimately rather than claiming to review everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a reputation as the go-to reviewer for specific genres; review many titles in those areas and stay up to date with trends. Specialization makes editors more likely to assign you relevant books and strengthens your pitch credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put together a packet of your best reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble a ‘greatest hits’ packet of your strongest work to show editors who don't know you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a mix of recognizable traditionally published titles and indie books to demonstrate range. Keep this packet updated as you get published in more prestigious outlets. Use it when querying editors to showcase your maximum potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Join an association
rubrics_metrics.description: Participate in professional communities (e.g., National Book Critic’s Circle) to access resources and networking opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memberships (example: $50/year for freelancers) can provide resources, fellowships (Emerging Critics), and credibility. Being part of a community helps career development and visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find out upcoming releases (pitch months in advance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan ahead by tracking publishers’ catalogs and pitching reviews well before publication dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazines and papers typically run reviews close to a book’s release; obtain publisher catalogs (PDFs from Penguin, etc.) or contact publishers for upcoming lists. Create a shortlist of upcoming books suited to your beats and outlets to pitch months ahead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start small-ish (build up from modest outlets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Target smaller local papers, online magazines, and certain literary journals before aiming for top national outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realistically target modest opportunities initially; compile a hit list of outlets and suitable upcoming books for each. Use early placements to build credentials and work toward larger publications over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch reviews effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Send focused, well-researched pitches that sell the story your review would tell and demonstrate why you’re the right reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the correct editor (don’t send to unrelated desks). Pitch the narrative or news angle that makes the book worth reviewing: newsworthiness, anniversaries, zeitgeist relevance, or category momentum. Explain why you should review it by linking to samples and showing subject-matter knowledge. Pitch early; editors assign reviews weeks or months in advance. Example guidance: a successful pitch can reference personal or topical connections relevant to the title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always follow up politely
rubrics_metrics.description: Send a short, polite reminder if you don’t receive a reply after about two weeks, and be gracious if rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat follow-ups as basic professionalism — emails get lost. If an outlet says 'no thank you,' respond courteously and leave a positive impression; future suitable opportunities may arise because of your professionalism. Persistence plus politeness is advised.
